{{Short description|Type of probability distribution}}
 
In [[probability theory]], a '''subgaussian distribution''', the distribution of a '''subgaussian random variable''', is a [[probability distribution]] with strong tail decay. More specifically, the tails of a subgaussian distribution are dominated by (i.e. decay at least as fast as) the tails of a [[Gaussian distribution|Gaussian]]. This property gives subgaussian distributions their name. 

Often in analysis, we divide an object (such as a random variable) into two parts, a central bulk and a distant tail, then analyze each separately. In probability, this division usually goes like "Everything interesting happens near the center. The tail event is so rare, we may safely ignore that." Subgaussian distributions are worthy of study, because the gaussian distribution is well-understood, and so we can give sharp bounds on the rarity of the tail event. An analogous class, sometimes called [[Subexponential distribution (light-tailed)|subexponential distributions]], is also useful; note however that the [[heavy-tailed distribution#subexponential distributions|more established meaning of subexponential]] is almost the opposite -- that decay is ''slower'' than exponential rather than that the tail is ''lighter'' than exponential -- and so care must be taken with that term. 

Formally, the probability distribution of a random variable ''<math>X </math>'' is called subgaussian if there is a positive [[Constant (mathematics)|constant]] ''C'' such that for every <math>t \geq 0</math>,

: <math display="inline">
\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) \leq 2 \exp{(-t^2/C^2)}
</math>.
There are many equivalent definitions. For example, a random variable ''<math>X</math>'' is sub-Gaussian iff its distribution function is bounded from above (up to a constant) by the distribution function of a Gaussian:

:<math>\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) \leq c\, \mathbb{P}(|Z| \geq t) \quad \forall t > 0</math>

where <math>c\ge 0</math> is constant and <math>Z</math> is a mean zero Gaussian random variable.{{r|Wainwright2019|at=Theorem 2.6}}

== Definitions ==

=== Subgaussian norm ===
The '''subgaussian norm''' of <math>X </math>, denoted as <math>\Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2} </math>, is<math display="block">\Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2} = \inf\left\{ c>0 : \mathbb{E}\left[\exp{\left(\frac{X^2}{c^2}\right)}\right] \leq 2 \right\}.</math>In other words, it is the [[Orlicz space|Orlicz norm]] of <math>X </math> generated by the Orlicz function <math>\Phi(u)=e^{u^2}-1. </math> By condition <math>(2)</math> below, subgaussian random variables can be characterized as those random variables with finite subgaussian norm.

=== Variance proxy ===
If there exists a number <math>s^2 \ge 0</math> such that <math>\mathbb{E} [e^{(X-\mathbb{E}[X])t}] \leq e^{\frac{s^2t^2}{2}}</math> for all <math>t \in \mathbb{R}</math>, then <math>s^2</math> is called a ''variance proxy''. The smallest such <math>s^2</math> is called the ''optimal variance proxy'' and denoted by <math>\Vert X\Vert_{\mathrm{vp}}^2</math>.

The optimal variance proxy and the subgaussian norm are related by
<math display="block"> \sqrt{3/8} \cdot \Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2} \leq \Vert X\Vert_{\mathrm{vp}} \leq \sqrt{\log 2} \cdot \Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2},</math>
and both bounds are sharp, attained by the standard Gaussian and Rademacher distributions,
respectively.<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last=Leskelä
 |first=Lasse
 |last2=Zhukov
 |first2=Matvei
 |year=2026
 |title=Sharp constants relating the sub-Gaussian norm and the sub-Gaussian parameter
 |journal=Electronic Communications in Probability
 |volume=31
 |pages=1–11
 |doi=10.1214/26-ECP761
 |doi-access=free
}}
</ref>

For a Gaussian random variable <math>X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)</math>, one has <math>\mathbb{E}[e^{(X-\mathbb{E}[X])t}] = e^{\frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}}</math>, and therefore <math>\|X\|_{\mathrm{vp}}^2 = \sigma^2</math>.

=== Equivalent definitions ===
Let ''<math>X </math>'' be a random variable with zero mean. Let <math>K_1, K_2, K_3, \dots</math> be positive constants. The following conditions are equivalent: (Proposition 2.5.2 <ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Vershynin |first=R. |title=High-dimensional probability: An introduction with applications in data science |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2018 |location=Cambridge}}</ref>)

# Tail probability bound: <math>
\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) \leq 2 \exp{(-t^2/K_1^2)}
</math> for all <math>t \geq 0</math>;
# Finite subgaussian norm: <math>\Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2} = K_2 < \infty</math>; 
# [[Moment (mathematics)|Moment]]: <math>\mathbb{E} |X|^p \leq 2K_3^p \Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right)</math> for all ''<math>p \geq 1</math>'', where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Gamma function]];
# [[Moment (mathematics)|Moment]]: <math>\mathbb{E}|X|^p\leq K^p p^{p/2}</math> for all <math>p \geq 1</math>;
# [[Moment-generating function]] (of ''<math>X </math>''), or variance proxy{{R|kahane}}{{R|buldygin}} : <math>\mathbb{E} [e^{(X-\mathbb{E}[X])t}] \leq e^{\frac{K^2t^2}{2}}</math> for all <math>t</math>;
# [[Moment-generating function]] (of ''<math>X^2 </math>''): <math>\mathbb{E}[e^{X^2t^2}] \leq e^{K^2t^2}</math> for all <math>t \in [-1/K, +1/K]</math>;
#  [[Union bound]]: for some ''c > 0'', <math> \ \mathbb{E}[\max\{|X_1 - \mathbb{E}[X]|,\ldots,|X_n - \mathbb{E}[X]|\}] \leq c \sqrt{\log n}</math> for all ''n > c'', where <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|i.i.d]] copies of ''X'';
#  [[Subexponential distribution (light-tailed)|Subexponential]]: <math>X^2</math> has a subexponential distribution.
Furthermore, the constant <math>K</math> is the same in the definitions (1) to (5), up to an absolute constant. So for example, given a random variable satisfying (1) and (2), the minimal constants <math>K_1, K_2</math> in the two definitions satisfy <math>K_1 \leq cK_2, K_2 \leq c' K_1</math>, where <math>c, c'</math> are constants independent of the random variable.

=== Proof of equivalence ===
As an example, the first four definitions are equivalent by the proof below.

''Proof''. <math>(1)\implies(3)</math> By the [[layer cake representation]],<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbb{E} |X|^p &= \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(|X|^p \geq t) dt\\
&= \int_0^\infty pt^{p-1}\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) dt\\
&\leq 2\int_0^\infty pt^{p-1}\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{K_1^2}\right) dt\\
\end{align}</math>


After a change of variables <math>u=t^2/K_1^2</math>, we find that<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbb{E} |X|^p &\leq 2K_1^p \frac{p}{2}\int_0^\infty u^{\frac{p}{2}-1}e^{-u} du\\
&= 2K_1^p \frac{p}{2}\Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)\\
&= 2K_1^p \Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right).
\end{align}</math><math>(3)\implies(2)</math> By the [[Taylor series]] <math display="inline">e^x = 1 + \sum_{p=1}^\infty \frac{x^p}{p!},</math><math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}[\exp{(\lambda X^2)}] &= 1 + \sum_{p=1}^\infty \frac{\lambda^p \mathbb{E}{[X^{2p}]}}{p!}\\
&\leq 1 + \sum_{p=1}^\infty \frac{2\lambda^p K_3^{2p} \Gamma\left(p+1\right)}{p!}\\
&= 1 + 2 \sum_{p=1}^\infty \lambda^p K_3^{2p}\\
&= 2 \sum_{p=0}^\infty \lambda^p K_3^{2p}-1\\
&= \frac{2}{1-\lambda K_3^2}-1 \quad\text{for }\lambda K_3^2 <1,
\end{align}</math>which is less than or equal to <math>2</math> for <math>\lambda \leq \frac{1}{3K_3^2}</math>. Let <math>K_2 \geq 3^{\frac{1}{2}}K_3</math>, then <math display="inline">\mathbb{E}[\exp{(X^2/K_2^2)}] \leq 2.</math>


<math>(2)\implies(1)</math> By [[Markov's inequality]],<math display="block">\mathbb{P}(|X|\geq t) = \mathbb{P}\left( \exp\left(\frac{X^2}{K_2^2}\right) \geq \exp\left(\frac{t^2}{K_2^2}\right) \right) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\exp{(X^2/K_2^2)}]}{\exp\left(\frac{t^2}{K_2^2}\right)} \leq 2 \exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{K_2^2}\right). </math><math>(3) \iff (4)</math> by asymptotic formula for gamma function: <math>\Gamma(p/2 + 1 ) \sim \sqrt{\pi p} \left(\frac{p}{2e} \right)^{p/2}</math>.

From the proof, we can extract a cycle of three inequalities:

* If <math>
\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) \leq 2 \exp{(-t^2/K^2)}
</math>, then <math>\mathbb{E} |X|^p \leq 2K^p \Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right)</math> for all <math>p \geq 1 </math>.
* If <math>\mathbb{E} |X|^p \leq 2K^p \Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right)</math> for all <math>p \geq 1 </math>, then <math>\|X \|_{\psi_2} \leq 3^{\frac{1}{2}}K  </math>.
* If <math>\|X \|_{\psi_2} \leq K  </math>, then <math>
\mathbb{P}(|X| \geq t) \leq 2 \exp{(-t^2/K^2)}
</math>.

In particular, the constant <math>K </math> provided by the definitions are the same up to a constant factor, so we can say that the definitions are equivalent up to a constant independent of <math>X</math>.

Similarly, because up to a positive multiplicative constant, <math>\Gamma(p/2 + 1) =  p^{p/2} \times ((2e)^{-1/2}p^{1/2p})^p</math> for all <math>p \geq 1</math>, the definitions (3) and (4) are also equivalent up to a constant.

== Basic properties ==

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = * If <math display="inline">X</math> is subgaussian, and <math display="inline">k > 0</math>, then <math display="inline">\|kX\|_{\psi_2} = k \|X\|_{\psi_2}</math> and <math display="inline">\|kX\|_{vp} = k \|X\|_{vp}</math>.

* (Triangle inequality) If <math display="inline">X, Y</math> are subgaussian, then <math display="block">\|X+Y\|_{vp}^2 \leq (\|X\|_{vp} + \|Y\|_{vp})^2</math>

* (Chernoff bound) If <math display="inline">X</math> is subgaussian, then <math display="block">\mathbb{P}(X \geq t) \leq e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\|X\|_{vp}^2}}</math> for all <math display="inline">t \geq 0</math>
| name = Basic properties
}}

<math display="inline">X \lesssim X'</math> means that <math display="inline">X \leq CX'</math>, where the positive constant <math display="inline">C</math> is independent of <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">X'</math>.

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">X</math> is subgaussian, then <math display="block">\|X - \mathbb{E}[X]\|_{\psi_2} \lesssim \|X\|_{\psi_2}</math>
| name = Subgaussian deviation bound
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= By triangle inequality, <math>\|X - \mathbb{E}[X]\|_{\psi_2} \leq \|X\|_{\psi_2} + \|\mathbb{E}[X]\|_{\psi_2}</math>. Now we have <math>\|\mathbb{E}[X]\|_{\psi_2} = \sqrt{\ln 2} |\mathbb{E}[X]| \leq \sqrt{\ln 2} \mathbb{E}[|X|] \sim \mathbb{E}[|X|]</math>. By the equivalence of definitions (2) and (4) of subgaussianity, we have <math>\mathbb{E}[|X|] \lesssim \|X\|_{\psi_2}</math>.}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">X, Y</math> are subgaussian and independent, then <math display="block">\|X+Y\|_{vp}^2 \leq \|X\|_{vp}^2 + \|Y\|_{vp}^2</math>
| name = Independent subgaussian sum bound
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= If independent, then use that the cumulant of independent random variables is additive. That is, <math>\ln \mathbb{E}[e^{t(X+Y)}] = \ln \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] + \ln \mathbb{E}[e^{tY}]</math>.

If not independent, then by Hölder's inequality, for any <math>1/p + 1/q = 1</math> we have  
<math display="block">\mathbb{E}[e^{t(X+Y)}] = \|e^{t(X+Y)}\|_1 \leq e^{\frac 12 t^2 (p \|X\|_{vp}^2 + q \|Y\|_{vp}^2)}</math>  
Solving the optimization problem  
<math>\begin{cases}
\min p \|X\|_{vp}^2 + q \|Y\|_{vp}^2 \\
1/p + 1/q = 1
\end{cases}</math>, we obtain the result.}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Linear sums of subgaussian random variables are subgaussian.
| name = Corollary
}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">\mathbb{E}[X] = 0, \mathbb{E}[X^2] =1</math>, and <math display="inline">-\ln \mathbb{P}(X \geq t) \geq \frac 12 at^2</math> for all <math display="inline">t >0</math>, then <math display="block">\ln \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] \leq C_at^2</math> where <math display="inline">C_a > 0</math> depends on <math display="inline">a</math> only.
| name = Partial converse
| note = Matoušek 2008, Lemma 2.4
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 

Let <math display="inline">F(x)</math> be the CDF of <math display="inline">X</math>. The proof splits the integral of MGF to two halves, one with <math display="inline">tX > 1</math> and one with <math display="inline">tX \leq 1</math>, and bound each one respectively.

<math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] 
 &= \int_\R e^{tx} dF(x) \\
 &= \int_{-\infty}^{1/t} e^{tx} dF(x) + \int_{1/t}^{+\infty} e^{tx} dF(x) \\
 \end{aligned}
 </math>
Since <math display="inline">e^x \leq 1+x+x^2</math> for <math display="inline">x \leq 1</math>, <math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_{-\infty}^{1/t} e^{tx} dF(x) 
 &\leq \int_{-\infty}^{1/t} (1+tx + t^2x^2) dF(x)  \\
 &\leq \int_{\R} (1+tx + t^2x^2) dF(x)  \\
 &= 1 + t\mathbb{E}[X] + t^2 \mathbb{E}[X^2] \\
 &= 1 + t^2 \\
 &\leq e^{t^2}
 \end{aligned}
 </math>
For the second term, upper bound it by a summation: <math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_{1/t}^{+\infty} e^{tx} dF(x)
 &\leq e^2 \mathbb{P}(X \in [1/t, 2/t]) + e^3 \mathbb{P}(X \in [1/t, 2/t]) + \dots \\
 &\leq \sum_{k=1}^\infty e^{k+1} \mathbb{P}(X \geq k/t) \\
 &\leq \sum_{k=1}^\infty e^{k(2-\frac 12 ak/t^2)}
 \end{aligned}
 </math>
When <math display="inline">t\le \sqrt{a/8}</math>, for any <math display="inline">k\ge1</math>, <math display="inline">2k - \frac{a k^2}{2t^2} \le -\frac{ak}{4t^2}</math>, so

<math display="block">
      \leq \frac{1}{e^{\frac{a}{4t^2}} - 1} \leq \frac 4a t^2
      </math>
When <math display="inline">t> \sqrt{a/8}</math>, by drawing out the curve of <math display="inline">f(x) = e^{-\frac{a}{2t^2}x^2 + 2x}</math>, and plotting out the summation, we find that <math display="block">
 \sum_{k=1}^\infty e^{k(2-\frac 12 ak/t^2)} \leq \int_\R f(x)dx + 2 \max_x f(x) = e^{\frac{2 t^2}{a}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 \pi t^2}{a}}+2\right) < 10 \sqrt{t^2/a} e^{\frac{2 t^2}{a}}
 </math> Now verify that <math display="inline">\ln 10 + \frac 12 \ln(t^2/a) + \frac{2}{a}t^2 < C_a t^2</math>, where <math display="inline">C_a</math> depends on <math display="inline">a</math> only.
}}{{hidden end}}

{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary
| note = Matoušek 2008, Lemma 2.2
| math_statement = <math display="inline">X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are independent random variables with the same upper subgaussian tail: <math display="block">
 -\ln \mathbb{P}(X_i \geq t) \geq \frac 12 at^2
 </math> for all <math display="inline">t>0</math>. Also, <math display="inline">\mathbb{E}[X_i] = 0, \mathbb{E}[X_i^2] = 1</math>, then for any unit vector <math display="inline">v\in \R^n</math>, the linear sum <math display="inline">\sum_i v_i X_i</math> has a subgaussian tail:<br />
<math display="block">
 -\ln \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_i v_i X_i \geq t \right) \geq C_a t^2
 </math> where <math display="inline">C_a > 0</math> depends only on <math display="inline">a</math>.
}}



== Concentration ==

{{Math theorem|name=Gaussian concentration inequality for Lipschitz functions|note=Tao 2012, Theorem 2.1.12.|math_statement=

If <math display="inline">f: \R^n \to \R</math> is <math display="inline">L</math>-Lipschitz, and <math display="inline">X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)</math> is a standard gaussian vector, then <math display="inline">f(X)</math> concentrates around its expectation at a rate <math display="block">
      \mathbb{P}(f(X) - \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \geq t)\leq e^{-\frac{2}{\pi^2}\frac{t^2}{L^2}}
      </math> and similarly for the other tail.
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
By shifting and scaling, it suffices to prove the case where <math display="inline">L = 1</math>, and <math display="inline">\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = 0</math>.

Since every 1-Lipschitz function is uniformly approximable by 1-Lipschitz smooth functions (by convolving with a mollifier), it suffices to prove it for 1-Lipschitz smooth functions.

Now it remains to bound the cumulant generating function.

To exploit the Lipschitzness, we introduce <math display="inline">Y</math>, an independent copy of <math display="inline">X</math>, then by Jensen, <math display="block">
          \mathbb{E}[e^{t(X-Y)}] = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\mathbb{E}[e^{-tY}] \geq \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]e^{-t\mathbb{E}[Y]} = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]
          </math> 

By the circular symmetry of gaussian variables, we introduce <math display="inline">X_\theta := Y\cos\theta + X\sin\theta</math>. This has the benefit that its derivative <math display="inline">X' = -Y\sin\theta + X\cos\theta</math> is independent of it.

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}e^{t(f(X) - f(Y))} 
          &=e^{t(f(X_{\pi/2}) - f(X_0))} \\
          &= e^{t\int_0^{\pi/2} \nabla f(X_\theta) \cdot X_\theta'd\theta} \\
          &= e^{\pi t/2 \int_0^{\pi/2} \nabla f(X_\theta) \cdot X_\theta'\frac{d\theta}{\pi/2}} \\
          &\leq \int_0^{\pi/2}  e^{\pi t/2 \nabla f(X_\theta) \cdot X_\theta'}\frac{d\theta}{\pi/2} \\
          \end{aligned}</math>

Now take its expectation, <math display="block">
          \mathbb{E}[e^{t(f(X) - f(Y))}] \leq \int_0^{\pi/2} \mathbb{E}[e^{\pi t/2 \nabla f(X_\theta) \cdot X_\theta'}]\frac{d\theta}{\pi/2} 
          </math> The expectation within the integral is over the joint distribution of <math display="inline">X, Y</math>, but since the joint distribution of <math display="inline">X_\theta, X_\theta'</math> is exactly the same, we have

<math display="block">
          = \mathbb{E}_X[\mathbb{E}_Y[e^{\pi t/2 \nabla f(X) \cdot Y}]]
          </math> 

Conditional on <math display="inline">X</math>, the quantity <math display="inline">\nabla f(X) \cdot Y</math> is normally distributed, with variance <math display="inline">\leq 1</math>, so <math display="block">
          \leq e^{\frac 12 (\pi t/2)^2} = e^{\frac{\pi^2}{8} t^2}
          </math>

Thus, we have <math display="block">
          \ln \mathbb{E}[e^{tf(X)}] \leq \frac{\pi^2}{8}t^2
          </math>
}}{{hidden end}}


== Strictly subgaussian ==
Expanding the [[cumulant generating function]]:<math display="block">\frac 12 s^2 t^2 \geq \ln \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \frac 12 \mathrm{Var}[X] t^2 + \kappa_3 t^3 + \cdots</math>we find that <math>\mathrm{Var}[X] \leq \|X\|_{\mathrm{vp}}^2</math>. At the edge of possibility, we define that a random variable <math>X</math> satisfying <math>\mathrm{Var}[X]=\|X\|_{\mathrm{vp}}^2</math> is called ''strictly'' subgaussian.

=== Properties ===


'''Theorem.'''<ref name=":2">{{cite arXiv |last1=Bobkov |first1=S. G. |title=Strictly subgaussian probability distributions |date=2023-08-03 |eprint=2308.01749 |last2=Chistyakov |first2=G. P. |last3=Götze |first3=F.|class=math.PR }}</ref> Let <math>X</math> be a subgaussian random variable with mean zero. If all zeros of its [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] are real, then <math>X</math> is strictly subgaussian.

'''Corollary.''' If <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are independent and strictly subgaussian, then any linear sum of them is strictly subgaussian.

=== Examples ===
By calculating the characteristic functions, we can show that some distributions are strictly subgaussian: symmetric uniform distribution, symmetric [[Bernoulli distribution]].

Since a symmetric uniform distribution is strictly subgaussian, its convolution with itself is strictly subgaussian. That is, the symmetric [[triangular distribution]] is strictly subgaussian.

Since the symmetric Bernoulli distribution is strictly subgaussian, any symmetric [[Binomial distribution]] is strictly subgaussian.

The optimal variance proxy <math>\Vert X\Vert_{\mathrm{vp}}^2</math> is known for many standard probability distributions, including the beta, Bernoulli, Dirichlet{{R|marchal2017}}, Kumaraswamy, triangular{{R|arbel2020}}, truncated Gaussian, and truncated exponential.{{R|barreto2024}}

=== Bernoulli distribution ===
Let <math>p + q = 1</math> be two positive numbers. Let <math>X </math> be a centered Bernoulli distribution <math>p\delta_q + q \delta_{-p}</math>, so that it has mean zero, then <math>\Vert X\Vert_{\mathrm{vp}}^2 = \frac{p-q}{2(\log p-\log q)}</math>.<ref name=":2" /> Its subgaussian norm is <math>t</math> where <math>t</math> is the unique positive solution to <math>pe^{(q/t)^2} + qe^{(p/t)^2} = 2</math>.

Let ''<math>X </math>'' be a random variable with symmetric Bernoulli distribution (or [[Rademacher distribution]]). That is, ''<math>X </math>'' takes values <math>-1 </math> and <math>1 </math> with probabilities <math>1/2 </math> each. Since ''<math>X^2=1 </math>'', it follows that<math display="block">\Vert X \Vert_{\psi_2} = \inf\left\{ c>0 : \mathbb{E}\left[\exp{\left(\frac{X^2}{c^2}\right)}\right] \leq 2 \right\} = \inf\left\{ c>0 : \exp{\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\right)} \leq 2 \right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln 2}}, </math>and hence ''<math>X </math>'' is a subgaussian random variable.

=== Bounded distributions ===
[[File:Bounded probability distributions, compared with the normal distribution.svg|thumb|Some commonly used bounded distributions.]]
Bounded distributions have no tail at all, so clearly they are subgaussian.

If <math>X</math> is bounded within the interval <math>[a, b]</math>, [[Hoeffding's lemma]] states that <math>\Vert X\Vert_{\mathrm{vp}}^2 \leq \left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)^2 </math>. [[Hoeffding's inequality]] is the Chernoff bound obtained using this fact.

=== Convolutions ===
[[File:Gaussian-mixture-example.svg|thumb|Density of a mixture of three normal distributions (''μ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5, 10, 15, ''σ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2) with equal weights. Each component is shown as a weighted density (each integrating to 1/3)]]
Since the sum of subgaussian random variables is still subgaussian, the convolution of subgaussian distributions is still subgaussian. In particular, any convolution of the normal distribution with any bounded distribution is subgaussian.

=== Mixtures ===
Given subgaussian distributions <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n</math>, we can construct an additive mixture <math>X</math> as follows: first randomly pick a number <math>i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}</math>, then pick <math>X_i</math>.

Since <math>\mathbb{E}\left[\exp{\left(\frac{X^2}{c^2}\right)}\right] = \sum_i p_i \mathbb{E}\left[\exp{\left(\frac{X_i^2}{c^2}\right)}\right] </math>we have <math>\|X\|_{\psi_2} \leq \max_i \|X_i\|_{\psi_2}</math>, and so the mixture is subgaussian.

In particular, any [[Mixture distribution|gaussian mixture]] is subgaussian.

More generally, the mixture of infinitely many subgaussian distributions is also subgaussian, if the subgaussian norm has a finite [[Infimum and supremum|supremum]]: <math>\|X\|_{\psi_2} \leq \sup_i \|X_i\|_{\psi_2}</math>.

== Subgaussian random vectors ==
So far, we have discussed subgaussianity for real-valued random variables. We can also define subgaussianity for [[Multivariate random variable|random vectors]]. The purpose of subgaussianity is to make the tails decay fast, so we generalize accordingly: a subgaussian random vector is a random vector where the tail decays fast.

Let <math>X </math> be a random vector taking values in <math>\R^n</math>.

'''Define.'''

* <math>\|X\|_{\psi_2} := \sup_{v \in S^{n-1}}\|v^T X\|_{\psi_2}</math>, where <math>S^{n-1}</math> is the [[unit sphere]] in <math>\R^n</math>. Similarly for the variance proxy <math>\|X\|_{vp} := \sup_{v \in S^{n-1}}\|v^T X\|_{vp}</math>
* <math>X </math> is subgaussian iff <math>\|X\|_{\psi_2} < \infty</math>.

'''Theorem.''' (Theorem 3.4.6 <ref name=":0" />) For any positive integer <math>n</math>, the uniformly distributed random vector <math>X \sim U(\sqrt{n} S^{n-1}) </math> is subgaussian, with <math>\|X\|_{\psi_2} \lesssim{} 1</math>.

This is not so surprising, because as <math>n \to \infty</math>, the projection of <math> U(\sqrt{n} S^{n-1}) </math> to the first coordinate [[Convergence of random variables|converges in distribution]] to the standard normal distribution.

== Maximum inequalities ==


{{Math theorem
| math_statement = 
If <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are mean-zero subgaussians, with <math>\|X_i \|_{vp}^2 \leq \sigma^2</math>, then for any <math>\delta  > 0</math>, we have <math>\max(X_1, \dots, X_n) \leq \sigma\sqrt{2 \ln \frac{n}{\delta}}</math> with probability <math>\geq 1-\delta</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=  By the Chernoff bound, <math>\mathbb{P}(X_i \geq \sigma \sqrt{2 \ln(n/\delta)}) \leq \delta/n</math>. Now apply the [[union bound]]. }}


{{Math theorem
| note=Exercise 2.5.10 <ref name=":0" />
| math_statement = If <math>X_1, X_2, \dots</math> are subgaussians, with <math>\|X_i \|_{\psi_2} \leq K</math>, then <math display="block">\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_n \frac{|X_n|}{\sqrt{1+\ln n}}\right] \lesssim K, \quad \mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1 \leq n \leq N} |X_n|\right] \lesssim K \sqrt{\ln N}</math>Further, the bound is sharp, since when <math>X_1, X_2, \dots</math> are IID samples of <math>\mathcal N(0, 1)</math> we have <math>\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1 \leq n \leq N} |X_n|\right] \gtrsim \sqrt{\ln N}</math>.<ref>Kamath, Gautam. "[http://www.gautamkamath.com/writings/gaussian_max.pdf Bounds on the expectation of the maximum of samples from a gaussian]." (2015)</ref>
}}


{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math>X_1, \dots, X_n</math> are subgaussian, with <math>\|X_i \|_{vp}^2 \leq \sigma^2</math>, then<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\max_i (X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i])] \leq \sigma\sqrt{ 2\ln n}, &\quad \mathbb{P}(\max_i (X_i- \mathbb{E}[X_i]) > t) \leq n e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}}, \\
\mathbb{E}[\max_i |X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i]|] \leq \sigma\sqrt{ 2\ln (2n)},
&\quad
\mathbb{P}(\max_i |X_i- \mathbb{E}[X_i]| > t) \leq 2 n e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}}
\end{aligned}</math>
| note = over a finite set<ref>{{Cite web |title=MIT 18.S997 {{!}} Spring 2015 {{!}} High-Dimensional Statistics, Chapter 1. Sub-Gaussian Random Variables |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-s997-high-dimensional-statistics-spring-2015/a69e2f53bb2eeb9464520f3027fc61e6_MIT18_S997S15_Chapter1.pdf |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=MIT OpenCourseWare |language=en}}</ref>
}}
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= For any t>0:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\max_{1\le i\le n}(X_i-\mathbb{E}[X_i])\bigr]
&=\frac1t\,\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\ln\max_{i}e^{\,t(X_i-\mathbb{E}[X_i])}\Bigr]\\
&\le\frac1t\ln \mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\max_{i}e^{\,t(X_i-\mathbb{E}[X_i])}\Bigr] \quad \text{by Jensen}\\
&\le\frac1t\ln\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E} e^{t(X_i-\mathbb{E}[X_i])}\\
&\le\frac1t\ln\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\sigma^{2}t^{2}/2}\quad \text{by def of }\|\cdot\|_{vp}\\
&=\frac{\ln n}{t}+\frac{\sigma^{2}t}{2} \\
&\overset{t=\sqrt{2\ln n}/\sigma}{=}\;\sigma\sqrt{2\ln n},
\end{aligned}</math>This is a standard proof structure for proving [[Chernoff bound|Chernoff-like bounds]] for sub-Gaussian variables. For the second equation, it suffices to prove the case with one variable and zero mean, then use the [[union bound]]. First by [[Markov's inequality|Markov]], <math>\mathbb{P}(X > t) \leq \mathbb{P}(e^{sX}  > e^{st}) \leq e^{-st} \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}]
</math>, then by definition of variance proxy, <math>\leq e^{-st} e^{\sigma^2s^2/2}
</math>, and then optimize at <math>s = -t^2/2\sigma^2
</math>.
}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Fix a finite set of vectors <math>v_1, \dots, v_n</math>. If <math>X</math> is a random vector, such that each <math>\| v_i^T X \|_{vp}^2 \leq \sigma^2</math>, then the above 4 inequalities hold, with <math>\max_{v \in \mathrm{conv}(v_1, \dots, v_n)}(v^T X - \mathbb{E}[v^T X])</math> replacing <math>\max_i (X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i])</math>. Here, <math>\mathrm{conv}(v_1, \dots, v_n)</math> is the [[Convex hull|convex polytope hulled]] by the vectors <math>v_1, \dots, v_n</math>.
| note = over a [[convex polytope]]
| name=Corollary
}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = If <math>X</math> is a random vector in <math>\R^d</math>, such that <math>\|v^T X\|_{vp}^2 \leq \sigma^2</math> for all <math>v</math> on the unit sphere <math>S</math>, then <math display="block">\mathbb{E}[\max_{v \in S} v^T X] = \mathbb{E}[\max_{v \in S} |v^T X|] \leq 4\sigma \sqrt{d} </math>For any <math>\delta > 0</math>, with probability at least <math>1-\delta</math>,<math display="block">\max_{v \in S} v^T X = \max_{v \in S} | v^T X | \leq 4 \sigma \sqrt{d}+2 \sigma \sqrt{2 \log (1 / \delta)}</math>
| note = subgaussian random vectors
}}

== Inequalities ==
'''Theorem.''' (Theorem 2.6.1 <ref name=":0" />) There exists a positive constant <math>C</math> such that given any number of independent mean-zero subgaussian random variables <math>X_1, \dots,X_n</math>, <math display="block">\left\|\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right\|_{\psi_2}^2 \leq C \sum_{i=1}^n\left\|X_i\right\|_{\psi_2}^2</math>'''Theorem.''' (Hoeffding's inequality) (Theorem 2.6.3 <ref name=":0" />) There exists a positive constant <math>c</math> such that given any number of independent mean-zero subgaussian random variables <math>X_1, \dots,X_N</math>,<math display="block">\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right| \geq t\right) \leq 2 \exp \left(-\frac{c t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^N\left\|X_i\right\|_{\psi_2}^2}\right)
\quad \forall t > 0</math>'''Theorem.''' (Bernstein's inequality) (Theorem 2.8.1 <ref name=":0" />) There exists a positive constant <math>c</math> such that given any number of independent mean-zero subexponential random variables <math>X_1, \dots,X_N</math>,<math display="block">\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right| \geq t\right) \leq 2 \exp \left(-c \min \left(\frac{t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^N\left\|X_i\right\|_{\psi_1}^2}, \frac{t}{\max _i\left\|X_i\right\|_{\psi_1}}\right)\right)</math>
'''Theorem.''' (Khinchine inequality) (Exercise 2.6.5 <ref name=":0" />) There exists a positive constant <math>C</math> such that given any number of independent mean-zero variance-one subgaussian random variables <math>X_1, \dots,X_N</math>, any <math>p \geq 2</math>, and any <math>a_1, \dots, a_N \in \R</math>,<math display="block">\left(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2\right)^{1 / 2} \leq\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N a_i X_i\right\|_{L^p} \leq C K \sqrt{p}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2\right)^{1 / 2}</math>

== Hanson-Wright inequality ==
The '''Hanson-Wright inequality''' states that if a random vector <math>X </math> is subgaussian in a certain sense, then any [[quadratic form]] <math>A</math> of this vector, <math>X^TAX</math>, is also subgaussian/subexponential. Further, the upper bound on the tail of <math>X^TAX</math>, is [[Uniform boundedness|uniform]].

A weak version of the following theorem was proved in (Hanson, Wright, 1971).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanson |first1=D. L. |last2=Wright |first2=F. T. |date=1971 |title=A Bound on Tail Probabilities for Quadratic Forms in Independent Random Variables |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=1079–1083 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177693335 |jstor=2240253 |issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free }}</ref> There are many extensions and variants. Much like the [[central limit theorem]], the Hanson-Wright inequality is more a cluster of theorems with the same purpose, than a single theorem. The purpose is to take a subgaussian vector and uniformly bound its quadratic forms.

'''Theorem.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Rudelson |first1=Mark |last2=Vershynin |first2=Roman |date=January 2013 |title=Hanson-Wright inequality and sub-gaussian concentration |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-communications-in-probability/volume-18/issue-none/Hanson-Wright-inequality-and-sub-gaussian-concentration/10.1214/ECP.v18-2865.full |journal=Electronic Communications in Probability |volume=18 |issue=none |pages=1–9 |doi=10.1214/ECP.v18-2865 |issn=1083-589X|arxiv=1306.2872 }}</ref>'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vershynin |first=Roman |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/highdimensional-probability/797C466DA29743D2C8213493BD2D2102 |title=High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-41519-4 |series=Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics |location=Cambridge |chapter=6. Quadratic Forms, Symmetrization, and Contraction |pages=127–146 |doi=10.1017/9781108231596.009 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108231596.009}}</ref> There exists a constant <math>c</math>, such that:

Let <math>n </math> be a positive integer. Let <math>X_1, ..., X_n</math> be [[Independence (probability theory)|independent random variables]], such that each satisfies <math>E[X_i] = 0</math>. Combine them into a random vector <math>X = (X_1, \dots, X_n)</math>. For any <math>n\times n</math> matrix <math>A</math>, we have<math display="block">\mathbb{P}(|X^T AX - \mathbb{E}[X^TAX]| > t ) \leq \max\left( 2 e^{-\frac{ct^2}{K^4\|A\|_F^2}}, 2 e^{-\frac{ct}{K^2\|A\|}} \right) = 
2 \exp \left[-c \min \left(\frac{t^2}{K^4\|A\|_F^2}, \frac{t}{K^2\|A\|}\right)\right]
</math>where <math>K = \max_i \|X_i\|_{\psi_2}</math>, and <math>\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{ij} A_{ij}^2}</math> is the [[Matrix norm#Frobenius norm|Frobenius norm]] of the matrix, and <math>\|A\| = \max_{\|x\|_2=1} \|Ax\|_2</math> is the [[operator norm]] of the matrix.

In words, the quadratic form <math>X^TAX</math> has its tail uniformly bounded by an exponential, or a gaussian, whichever is larger.


In the statement of the theorem, the constant <math>c</math> is an "absolute constant", meaning that it has no dependence on <math>n, X_1, \dots, X_n, A</math>. It is a [[mathematical constant]] much like ''pi'' and ''e''.

=== Consequences ===
'''Theorem''' (subgaussian concentration).'''<ref name=":1" />''' There exists a constant <math>c</math>, such that:

Let <math>n, m </math> be positive integers. Let <math>X_1, ..., X_n</math> be independent random variables, such that each satisfies <math>\mathbb{E}[X_i] = 0, \mathbb{E}[X_i^2] = 1</math>. Combine them into a random vector <math>X = (X_1, \dots, X_n)</math>. For any <math>m\times n</math> matrix <math>A</math>, we have<math display="block">\mathbb{P}( | \| AX\|_2 - \|A\|_F | > t ) \leq  2 e^{-\frac{ct^2}{K^4\|A\|^2}}</math>In words, the random vector <math>A X</math> is concentrated on a spherical shell of radius <math>\|A \|_F</math>, such that <math>\| AX\|_2 - \|A \|_F</math> is subgaussian, with subgaussian norm <math>\leq \sqrt{3/c} \|A\| K^2</math>.
